Empirical Research Plan – “Inequality, Changes in Inequality, and Subsequent Growth”

--------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------
Preferred strategy:  Two–stage least squares (panel IV) combined with an event-study/DID framework.

Rationale  
(a) Levels and changes in inequality are plausibly endogenous to growth (reverse causality, omitted institutions, measurement error).  
(b) A plausibly exogenous source of cross-country, time-varying inequality shocks exists: world-commodity price movements that interact with a country’s pre-sample commodity export structure.  These shocks predict within-country changes in the distribution of income (resource rents accrue disproportionately to capital owners and skilled labour, raising the Gini) but have limited direct mechanical effect on non-resource sectors’ future growth once contemporaneous terms-of-trade are controlled for.  
(c) A shift–share (Bartik-style) instrument satisfies conventional relevance tests, and the panel structure with country and period fixed effects nets out time-invariant heterogeneity and common shocks.  
(d) Staggered timing of “large inequality shocks” (≥ 5 Gini-point increase or decrease over a five-year window) lets us implement an event-study graph to show pre-trend equality and the subsequent growth path, providing a visual/diagnostic complement to the IV estimates.

--------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Continuous 1st-stage:  ΔIneq_it  =  Gini_i,t – Gini_i,t–5  
• Non-linear specification:  use a piece-wise spline or 3 quantile dummies of ΔIneq_it (large decreases, small/no change, large increases).

Instrument  
Shift–share “commodity inequality shock”:  

Z_it  =  ∑_k  (BaseShare_{ik,1990} × ΔWorldPrice_{k,t})  

where k indexes 36 internationally traded commodities.  BaseShare is the country’s net-export share in 1990 (pre-period).  

Control group / counterfactual  
Countries whose predicted inequality change Z_it is near zero in the same five-year period serve as the implicit counterfactual after we absorb country and period FE.

Treatment timing  
Five-year cells (e.g., 1981–85, 1986–90, …).  ΔIneq_it is measured in cell t; the outcome Growth_i,t+1 is the log-change in real GDP per-capita in the next five-year cell.

--------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument relevance – Commodity-price movements, interacted with historical export structure, cause within-country changes in inequality (supported by previous micro/labor-share evidence).  
A2. Exclusion – Conditional on contemporaneous terms-of-trade growth and full macro controls, Z_it affects future growth only through its effect on inequality, not through other channels (e.g., Dutch disease).  
A3. Parallel pre-trends (for DID/event study) – Countries about to experience large Z-induced inequality shocks do not already display diverging growth paths relative to controls in the pre-period.  
A4. Stable unit treatment (no cross-country spillovers) – One country’s commodity boom does not directly change another country’s growth, conditional on period FE.  
A5. Monotonicity – A positive Z_it weakly raises inequality in all countries (required for a well-defined LATE).

Plausibility  
A1 is empirically testable (first-stage F-statistic).  A2 is the most demanding but can be partially addressed by (i) controlling for contemporaneous and lagged TOT growth, (ii) dropping oil exporters in robustness, and (iii) over-identification tests using leave-one-out sector shares.  Pre-trend plots (event study) speak to A3.  A4 is reasonable given the small general-equilibrium effects at the 5-year horizon.  A5 is supported by prior evidence that positive commodity-price shocks raise top-income shares.

--------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------
Threat 1:  Violation of exclusion (commodity prices also affect investment or fiscal space).  
 Mitigation: add controls for log-terms-of-trade growth, government revenues from natural resources, investment/GDP, and interact commodity shock with export-to-GDP to absorb direct demand effects; re-estimate excluding top 5 resource exporters; placebo using agricultural-import shocks (which should affect prices but not inequality).

Threat 2:  Weak instrument in diversified economies.  
 Mitigation: report first-stage F; cluster-robust Anderson-Rubin test; construct leave-one-out Bartik to guard against mechanical correlation; use alternative baseline year (1985, 1995) to verify strength.

Threat 3:  Heterogeneous treatment effects / functional-form misspecification.  
 Mitigation: include cubic splines for ΔIneq_it and interactions with initial GDP or democracy; fully non-parametric binned scatter; test equality of coefficients across terciles.

--------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------
```r
# Load packages
library(data.table); library(fixest); library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------
d <- fread("inequality_growth_panel.csv")   # each row = country-year or 5-yr cell

# 2. Variable construction ------------------------------------
# Convert to 5-year cells
d[, period := floor(year/5)*5 ]
setkey(d, country, period)

# Inequality variables
d[, gini_lag := shift(gini, 1L, type = "lag"), by = country]
d[, d_ineq   := gini - gini_lag]                      # Δ inequality over 5 yrs

# Future growth outcome (lead)
d[, gdp_pc_lead := shift(log_gdp_pc, -1L, type = "lead"), by = country]
d[, growth_next := gdp_pc_lead - log_gdp_pc]          # growth in next 5-yr cell

# Instrument: commodity inequality shock
# Assume we already have commodity_price_k and base_share_k variables
price_vars   <- grep("^dprice_", names(d), value = TRUE)
share_vars   <- grep("^share_", names(d), value = TRUE)

d[, Z := rowSums(.SD[, ..price_vars] * .SD[, ..share_vars]), by = 1:nrow(d)]

# 3. Main IV regression ---------------------------------------
feols_main <- feols(growth_next ~ poly(d_ineq,3) + controls | country + period ~ Z,
                    data = d, cluster = ~country)

summary(feols_main, stage = 1)        # show 1st-stage F

# 4. Event-study diagnostic -----------------------------------
# Flag large inequality shock event (>5 Gini points up)
d[, treat := as.integer(d_ineq > 5)]
# Create event time k = -4,..,4 around first treatment
d[, first_treat_period := min(period[treat==1]), by = country]
d[, k := (period - first_treat_period)/5 ]

event_dt <- d[k >= -4 & k <= 4]
est <- feols(growth_next ~ i(k, ref = -1) | country + period, data = event_dt)
iplot(est) + ggtitle("Event-study: growth around inequality shock")

# 5. Robustness: exclude top 5 oil exporters ------------------
oil5 <- c("SAU","KWT","IRQ","IRN","RUS")
robust <- feols(growth_next ~ poly(d_ineq,3) + controls | country + period ~ Z,
                data = d[!country %in% oil5], cluster = ~country)
etable(list(main = feols_main, no_oil = robust))
```

--------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------
Theory gives ambiguous signs for inequality levels, but most political-economy and credit-constraint models predict that large *increases* in inequality in middle-income democracies depress future growth (negative coefficient for ΔIneq_it).  I expect:

• Semi-elasticity: a 5-point rise in the Gini (≈ 1 s.d.) lowers next-period 5-year growth by about 0.4 pp (≈ 0.08 pp annually).  
• Non-linearity: small inequality changes yield near-zero effect; negative effects kick in once ΔGini > 3–4 points; large decreases may also correlate with slower growth if driven by recessionary shocks, producing an ∩-shape.

--------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)

C1: Instrument relevance (F > 10) ................. 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction believable ............... 0.5  
C3: No differential pre-trends (event-study) ....... 0.8  
C4: No spillovers / SUTVA .......................... 0.8  
C5: Monotonicity (same sign effect of Z) ........... 0.7  

Total ≈ 3.8 / 5.  The main concern remains the exclusion restriction; multiple robustness and falsification tests are therefore critical.
